reading.body:
Self-hosted models shift the compute burden entirely onto the operator, meaning the power draw, the cooling, and the physical infrastructure become the operator's problem rather than a cloud vendor's.

The six tools here span the full stack from framework to inference runtime. PyTorch and TensorFlow provide the training and serialization layer. Hugging Face Transformers acts as the supply chain, distributing weights that the other tools consume. vLLM optimizes throughput for those weights on owned hardware. Ollama and llama.cpp push inference toward the edge and the laptop, trading raw throughput for portability and the absence of network data transfer. Each layer depends on the one below it, and all of them ultimately depend on the electricity and cooling available at the site where they run.

The notes attached to these tools emphasize model provenance, supply-chain verification, and the absence of external data sharing. Those concerns are governance concerns, not performance concerns. They explain why organizations choose self-hosted paths even when cloud inference would be simpler: the data never leaves a controlled facility. What the data does not cover is the actual hardware these tools run on, the power requirements of specific deployments, or any cost comparison between self-hosted and cloud inference. It records the software layer only.
